items.topic: Śiva's vibhu nature and sixfold form
items.gist: Śiva is eternal, all-pervading, and world-forming; his sixfold form and knowledge of space and sound lead to liberation.
Śiva's world-forming nature is marked by unboundedness and dissolution of limitation; his one dharma operates through svātantryaśakti.
Śakti is the self-form of being, mentally posited yet non-dual with Śiva; no real distinction exists between power and possessor.
In Śiva, anubhāva and vikalpa are not ordinary mental states; Śiva is known through his forms, not through sound or bindu alone.
Śiva's many powers include kalā, tattvas, creation, preservation, dissolution, grace, and the waking, dream, and sleep states.
The dharma of the whole tattva-group is the imperishable Self; knowledge abides in Śiva's nectar and pure awareness.
Rāma is the all-pervading Śiva, supreme cause; meditation and japa lead to the supreme Bhairava.
Differences of near and far arise through Śiva's svātantrya; the three powers are named svātantrya and manifest as icchā and related powers.
The name Mahābhairava is explained through Śiva's sustaining, illuminating, and fear-destroying functions.

items.topic: Etymology of Śiva and limited forms
items.gist: Śiva is praised as pati and beneficent Lord; limited forms of Rudra and others are partial manifestations of him.
Three powers appear in creation, preservation, dissolution, and the fourth; they expand into twelve and further cakra forms up to the sahasrāra.
Cakras are distinguished by their groups and functions, with goddess names assigned according to their operations.
The inner consciousness-form is worshipped as a cakra; Saṃviddevī nourishes it, and varṇas become bīja that clarify consciousness.
